notes: Ruling slot 22 holds the MPR (party-state born of the 1965 army coup); the ANC high command sits in coalition slot 13. MD's PPRD (2002) and ADFL (1996) are anachronistic and replaced; slot 23 keeps MD's House of Kilukeni. Name Zaire only from Oct 1971, so texts use Congo.

0.name: Groupe de Binza
0.text:
The Binza Group is the informal circle of Western-backed power brokers named after the Kinshasa suburb where its members met in the early 1960s. Mobutu himself, security chief Victor Nendaka, Justin Bomboko and banker Albert Ndele once decided the fate of governments from its villas; by 1970 the President has eased them into ministries, embassies and the central bank.

The group stands for a Congo firmly anchored to Washington and Brussels, with open doors for Western capital and a hard line against Lumumbists and Soviet influence. Its strength lies in personal ties to the American embassy, Belgian business and the security services, and in the conviction that Mobutu owes them his rise.

1.name: Convention Nationale Congolaise
1.text:
The Congolese National Convention is the coalition Moïse Tshombe assembled in 1965, when it won the parliamentary elections with dozens of allied parties. Banned with all other parties after Mobutu's coup, it lost its leader when Tshombe, kidnapped to Algeria in 1967, died in captivity in June 1969. Its old networks survive among Katangese notables and businessmen, with Godefroid Munongo held by the regime.

CONACO stands for federalism, provincial autonomy, private enterprise and close partnership with Belgium and the West. Its base lies in Katanga and among chiefs and traders of the south, and its leverage rests on memories of Tshombe's competence and the resentment of regions stripped of autonomy by Kinshasa.

2.name: Mouvement National Congolais–Kalonji
2.text:
The Congolese National Movement–Kalonji is the moderate wing that broke with Patrice Lumumba in 1959 under Albert Kalonji, Joseph Iléo and Cyrille Adoula. Its leader proclaimed the short-lived Mining State of South Kasai in 1960 and now lives in exile in Europe, while the party itself has been dissolved since 1966.

The movement favours a liberal, federal constitution, free enterprise, an independent judiciary and friendship with the West. Its following is concentrated among the Luba of Kasai and the educated middle class of Mbuji-Mayi and Kinshasa, and its leverage rests on the diamond economy of South Kasai and on Luba resentment of central rule.

3.name: Parti Solidaire Africain
3.text:
The African Solidarity Party was founded in 1959 in the Kwilu and Kwango districts and became one of the pillars of Lumumba's government. It split between Antoine Gizenga's radicals and the moderate wing of Cléophas Kamitatu, who served in Mobutu's early cabinets, and it has been dissolved since the party ban.

The moderate PSA tradition stands for a social state, rural development, cooperative agriculture, labour rights and parliamentary government, without breaking with the West. Its base lies among the Mbunda, Pende and Bambala peasants of Kwilu, teachers and clerks, and its leverage rests on a region that has already risen once in 1964 and still distrusts Kinshasa.

4.name: Mouvement National Congolais–Lumumba
4.text:
The Congolese National Movement–Lumumba is the party of Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister murdered in Katanga in January 1961. Banned since 1966, it survives as a network of veterans in Orientale and Kivu and in exile, while Mobutu has cynically proclaimed Lumumba a national hero to disarm his heirs.

The Lumumbists demand true economic independence, nationalisation of the mining trusts, a unitary state and close ties with the Soviet Union and the radical African states. Their base lies in Stanleyville, among Tetela and Swahili-speaking easterners and among students who revere Lumumba, and their leverage rests on the moral authority of a martyr whom no Congolese politician can openly reject.

5.name: Conseil National de Libération
5.text:
The National Liberation Council was formed in Brazzaville in 1963 by Lumumbist exiles and launched the Simba rebellion that in 1964 seized Stanleyville and half the country. Crushed by the national army, Belgian paratroopers and white mercenaries, it has dissolved into feuding exiles; Christophe Gbenye and Gaston Soumialot still claim its mantle.

The Council preaches a second independence through armed struggle, the overthrow of the pro-Western regime and the expulsion of foreign monopolies. Its remaining support lies among young militants of the east and in the bush, and its leverage rests on contacts in Brazzaville, Cairo and Dar es Salaam and on the possibility of rebuilding a rural guerrilla army.

6.name: Kitawala
6.text:
Kitawala is the clandestine prophetic movement that grew from the Watch Tower preaching brought from Northern Rhodesia in the 1920s. Persecuted by the Belgians, it survives in villages of Katanga, Kivu, Maniema and Orientale, refusing taxes, identity cards and the authority of chiefs and the state.

Its followers await the end of foreign domination and a world in which Africans will no longer serve white masters or their Congolese heirs. They reject missions, Western schooling and the post-colonial state alike, and hold to strict communal discipline. Kitawala has no formal leadership, but its leverage lies in its ability to empty villages of taxpayers and to feed rural revolt.

7.name: Jeunesse du Mouvement Populaire de la Révolution
7.english: Youth of the Popular Movement of the Revolution
7.native_full: Jeunesse du Mouvement Populaire de la Révolution
7.text:
The Youth of the Popular Movement of the Revolution is the single party's mass youth organisation, created after the N'Sele Manifesto of 1967 to absorb student unions and youth groups. After the bloody repression of the Lovanium student march of 4 June 1969, it is being imposed on campuses and schools as the only permitted association.

The JMPR mobilises rallies, cheers the Guide and polices neighbourhoods, schools and markets. Its rhetoric is anti-imperialist and populist, calling for a Congolese revolution free of foreign tutelage. Its base lies among unemployed urban youth and ambitious cadres, and its leverage rests on its brigades of vigilantes and its role as a recruiting ground for the party-state.

8.name: Shia Imami Ismaili Council for the Congo
8.english: Shia Imami Ismaili Council for the Congo
8.text:
The Shia Imami Ismaili Council for the Congo organises the small community of Ismaili traders of Indian origin settled in Kinshasa, Bukavu, Kisangani and Lubumbashi. Followers of the Aga Khan, they run shops, import houses and transport firms, linked by family to the large communities of Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.

The Council promotes education, health care and economic self-help under the Aga Khan's modernising guidance, while staying carefully loyal to whoever governs Kinshasa. It avoids politics, but its leverage lies in its commercial networks and capital, its links to East Africa and the Aga Khan's international institutions, and the value of its trading houses to regional economies.

9.name: Tujjar Kasai
9.text:
The Shia diamond merchants of Kasai are Lebanese families from Jabal Amil who have settled in Kananga, Tshikapa and Mbuji-Mayi since the colonial era. They buy and export diamonds, run trading posts and finance kin in southern Lebanon, where Imam Musa al-Sadr has just set up the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in 1969.

Younger traders follow al-Sadr's call for Shia dignity and organisation and look to the clerics of Najaf, among them Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim. Their leverage lies in money: they control much of the informal diamond trade and the cash that flows between Kasai, Antwerp and Beirut, and they can buy protection from officials and officers.

10.name: Wangwana wa Maniema
10.text:
The Wangwana of Maniema are the Swahili-speaking Muslim communities of Kasongo, Kindu, Kibombo and Kisangani, descended from the followers of the nineteenth-century Arab-Swahili traders. They form the oldest Muslim presence in the Congo, organised around local sheikhs, Quranic schools and mosques.

Their religious elders practise a conservative, quietist Sunni Islam of the Shafi'i school, loyal to the authorities and focused on teaching and community life. They seek recognition for Islam alongside the Catholic and Protestant churches, Quranic education and pilgrimage to Mecca. Their leverage lies in their discipline and trading networks along the river and in the east, where Swahili is the common language.

11.name: Warithi wa Tippu Tip
11.text:
The Heirs of Tippu Tip are a small circle of young Muslims of Maniema and Kisangani who invoke the Arab-Swahili trading empire that ruled the upper Congo before the Belgians. Some have studied in Zanzibar, Cairo or Mecca and returned with pan-Islamic pamphlets and radical ideas.

They denounce Christian missions and the Western-backed state as the heirs of colonial conquest, and dream of a united Muslim community stretching from the Indian Ocean to the Congo River under Islamic law. They have no recognised leader and little following, but their leverage lies in the grievances of a Muslim minority long marginalised by mission schools and colonial administrators.

12.name: Umoja wa Waislamu
12.text:
Muslim Unity is a reformist association of Muslim teachers, clerks and traders in Kinshasa, Kisangani and Bukavu who want to modernise a community left behind by colonial schooling. Inspired by Egyptian reformist literature and preachers trained at al-Azhar, they meet in mosques and private homes.

They call for Muslim schools teaching both religion and modern subjects, official recognition of Islam, charity funds for the poor and a moral renewal of public life. They avoid open confrontation with the regime but criticise corruption and the domination of the churches. Their leverage lies in their educated members and their growing role as spokesmen for Congolese Muslims.

13.name: Armée Nationale Congolaise
13.text:
The Congolese National Army is the force that grew from the mutinous Force Publique of 1960 and brought its commander Mobutu to power in the coup of 24 November 1965. Commanded by Lieutenant-General Louis Bobozo, it has crushed the Simba rebellion and the mercenary revolt with Western help, and remains the true foundation of the regime.

The high command defends national unity, order and its own privileges, distrusting both politicians and Lumumbist radicals. It relies on Belgian, American and Israeli advisers and equipment. Its base lies in the officer corps from Équateur and loyal paratroop units, and its leverage rests on its monopoly of force across a vast, barely governed country.

14.name: Église catholique au Congo
14.text:
The Catholic Church in the Congo is the largest institution in the country outside the state, with millions of faithful and most of its schools, hospitals and missions. Its leading figure is Joseph-Albert Malula, Archbishop of Kinshasa, created cardinal in 1969 and the first Congolese to hold that rank.

The Church defends Christian morality, its schools and the independence of religious life, and promotes an Africanised Catholicism. It supports order but watches the growing cult of the party with suspicion. Its base lies in parishes, seminaries and the educated elite it trained, and its leverage rests on its control of education and on Rome's international authority.
14.wiki: Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

15.name: Générale Congolaise des Minerais
15.text:
Gécomin is the state mining company created in 1967 when Mobutu nationalised the Belgian Union Minière du Haut-Katanga. It produces the copper and cobalt of Katanga that provide most of the Congo's export earnings, while technical management remains in the hands of the Belgian Société Générale des Minerais.

Around Gécomin gather managers, Belgian engineers, Kinshasa officials and businessmen who live on mining revenue, contracts and commissions. They want stable prices, foreign technical cooperation and a government that protects production. Their leverage is enormous: the copper revenues finance the state, the army and the patronage that holds the regime together.

16.name: Chambre de Commerce de Kinshasa
16.text:
The Kinshasa Chamber of Commerce brings together the merchants, importers and small industrialists of the capital, from Portuguese, Greek and Belgian trading houses to the first Congolese entrepreneurs. Its members prosper on the stabilisation of the economy after the 1967 currency reform introducing the zaire as monetary unit.

The Chamber calls for free trade, low taxes, legal security for private property and an end to arbitrary levies by officials and soldiers. It fears creeping state control of commerce and the favouritism of the party elite. Its leverage lies in its role in supplying the cities, its links to foreign banks and its taxes, which the treasury cannot do without.

17.name: Gardiens des Parcs
17.text:
The Park Guardians are the rangers, scientists and conservation officials who defend the national parks of the Congo, above all the former Albert National Park in Kivu, the oldest national park in Africa, and Garamba and Upemba. They have lived through rebellion, poaching and neglect since independence.

They call for protecting the mountain gorillas, elephants and forests, for strict control of hunting and for international support to the parks. They argue that wildlife is a national heritage and a future source of tourist income. Their numbers are small, but their leverage lies in international scientific and conservation networks and in the prestige the parks give the regime abroad.

18.name: Parti Lumumbiste Unifié
18.text:
The Unified Lumumbist Party was founded in 1964 by Antoine Gizenga, Lumumba's deputy prime minister, who led the rival Lumumbist government in Stanleyville in 1960–61. Banned like all parties, it survives clandestinely in Kwilu and Kinshasa while Gizenga lives in exile.

PALU stands for African socialism, land for peasants, nationalisation of strategic resources and a foreign policy of non-alignment free from both Western and Soviet tutelage. Its base lies among the Pende and Mbunda of Kwilu, poor urban workers and Lumumbist intellectuals, and its leverage rests on loyal village networks that have survived repression since the Mulelist uprising.

19.name: Parti de la Révolution Populaire
19.text:
The People's Revolutionary Party was founded in December 1967 by Laurent-Désiré Kabila, a veteran of the 1964 eastern rebellion who fought beside Che Guevara's Cubans. It holds a small liberated zone in the mountains of Fizi and Baraka near Lake Tanganyika, where it runs its own administration.

The PRP follows a Maoist line of protracted people's war, political education of peasants and self-reliance, rejecting both Western imperialism and Soviet revisionism. Its fighters are drawn mainly from the Bembe people. Its leverage lies in a resilient maquis the army has failed to destroy and in smuggling routes across the lake to Tanzania.

20.name: Front de Libération Nationale du Congo
20.english: Front for the National Liberation of the Congo
20.native_full: Front de Libération Nationale du Congo
20.text:
The Front for the National Liberation of the Congo was founded in 1968 by Nathanaël Mbumba among the former Katangese gendarmes who fled to Angola after Tshombe's fall. Several thousand strong, they serve the Portuguese colonial army against Angolan nationalists while waiting to return home in arms.

The Front draws on Lunda pride and resentment of Kinshasa, demanding autonomy or independence for Katanga and the overthrow of Mobutu. It speaks the language of regional patriotism rather than ideology. Its base lies among Lunda and southern Katangese communities, and its leverage rests on a trained army in exile on the border of the Congo's richest province.
20.wiki: Front for the National Liberation of the Congo

21.name: Les Affreux
21.text:
Les Affreux are the white mercenaries who fought for Katanga and later for Kinshasa against the Simba rebels, led by men such as Jean Schramme and Bob Denard. After their revolt at Bukavu in 1967 they were evacuated through Rwanda in 1968 and now wait in Europe and southern Africa for new contracts.

They combine anti-communism, colonial nostalgia and contempt for African self-government, and look to Portugal, Rhodesia and South Africa as allies. They have no political programme beyond war, pay and plunder. Their leverage lies in their battlefield record, their contacts with Katangese exiles and foreign intelligence services, and the willingness of some to hire them again.

22.name: Mouvement Populaire de la Révolution
22.text:
The Popular Movement of the Revolution is the single party founded by President Joseph-Désiré Mobutu with the N'Sele Manifesto of May 1967, eighteen months after the army coup that brought him to power. It is the only legal party under the 1967 constitution and is preparing presidential and legislative elections for late 1970.

The MPR preaches national unity, order, economic independence and loyalty to its founder, blending anti-colonial rhetoric with close cooperation with the United States and Belgium. Its base is the administration, the army and party cadres, and its leverage rests on control of the state, the copper revenues and the patronage that binds regional elites to the presidency.

23.name: House of Kilukeni
23.text:
The House of Kilukeni is the royal lineage of the old Kingdom of Kongo, whose kings ruled the lower Congo from Mbanza Kongo for centuries. Its title survives on the Angolan side of the border under Portuguese rule, but the Bakongo of the lower Congo still honour its memory.

Royalists dream of reuniting the Bakongo of the Congo, Angola and Congo-Brazzaville under a restored crown, an idea once championed by ABAKO and the late President Joseph Kasa-Vubu, who died in 1969. Their base lies among Bakongo elders and traditionalists, and their leverage rests on the deep cultural attachment of the Bakongo to their ancient kingdom.
